title: Consciousness and sleep
note: Consciousness is awareness of internal and external stimuli, and it shifts across the day. A roughly 24-hour circadian clock in the hypothalamus times sleep. Each night the brain cycles through NREM stages, from light sleep to deep slow-wave sleep, and REM sleep, when most vivid dreaming occurs.

read.title: A night in four stages
text: Sleep is not one steady state. Recordings of brain waves show that each night we pass through several cycles of distinct stages.

As you drift off, the fast beta waves of alert waking give way to slower alpha waves, then to theta waves in stage 1, a light, easily interrupted transition. Stage 2 is still theta-dominated but is marked by sleep spindles, brief bursts that may help memory, and K-complexes. Stage 3 is slow-wave sleep: big, slow delta waves, slowed heart rate and breathing, and the hardest time to wake someone.

Then comes REM sleep. The eyes dart under closed lids and the brain looks almost awake on an EEG, yet the voluntary muscles are paralyzed. This is when most vivid dreams happen. Across the night, REM periods grow longer, so much of a morning's sleep is REM.

Both kinds of sleep matter for learning. Slow-wave sleep after studying improves later performance, and REM is linked to memory and emotional processing. When people lose REM, they show REM rebound, spending extra time in it the next chance they get. That is one reason cramming all night can cost more than it gains.
